newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler cuts 1998 model year prices 0.6 percent.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler cuts 1998 model year prices 0.6 percent.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. announced Wednesday its average 1998 model year price will be down 0.6 percent, making it the only member of the U.S. Big Three automakers to slash prices amid an industry-wide price war.

Passenger car prices at Chrysler will be down 1.3 percent, while pickup trucks, minivans and sport/utilities will cost 0.4 percent less, the company said. All changes are based on comparably equipped models.
Ford Motor Co. said earlier this month its average 1998 model year price will be unchanged from a year ago. General Motors Corp.'s prices are going up 1.3 percent on average, the lowest in 10 years.
"This pricing reflects the realities of a competitive marketplace," said James Holden, executive vice president of sales and marketing at Chrysler.

Chrysler spokesman Mike McKesson said it is the first time in recent history the U.S. No. 3 automaker has cut its average starting model year prices. Both foreign and domestic automakers have been holding the line on prices this year in reaction to a fiercely competitive new vehicle market.

Prices disclosed Wednesday did not include how much Chrysler will charge for its redesigned 1998 Dodge Intrepid and Chrysler Concorde sedans, which are due out this fall. Also not included was the new Dodge Durango sport/utility vehicle.

In addition to cutting some base prices, Holden said Chrysler has raised other base prices to reflect option items that were added as standard equipment. Some option packages were also changed to better reflect what consumers are buying.

Chrysler said the Highline trim level for its 1998 Dodge and Plymouth Neon small car is now the base model. A Neon with air conditioning and automatic transmission, as well as more standard equipment, will cost $13,455, down from $13,770 for a comparably equipped 1997 model.
Chrysler lowered the prices on many of its Jeep Cherokee and Grand Cherokee sport/utility vehicles, and kept minivan prices mostly flat, McKesson said.

A four-wheel-drive Cherokee Sport with automatic transmission and the most popular option package will cost $22,070, including destination charge, a decrease of $805, or 3.5 percent, from the same 1997 model.
But Chrysler boosted the price on its popular line of Jeep Wranglers. A Wrangler Sport with a soft top and six-cylinder engine went up 1.9 percent to $20,145.
Chrysler also hiked the price of many of its full-size pickup trucks. A two-wheel-drive Dodge Ram pickup with a V-8 engine and short wheel base went up 3 percent, or $645, to $21,585.

Last year several automakers tried to keep price hikes modest and cut back on incentives. But incentives and other marketing programs have continued to rise. McKesson would not reveal Chrysler's incentive spending plans, but said they will continue to play a role in vehicle sales.
"It appears to us that incentives are something that seem to be part of the mix that make it possible for people to feel like they have received a value when they buy a car," he said.
